correctness.rationale: Expanding the degree count and motif count into indicators leaves covariance only when the selected host vertex belongs to the selected motif copy. Conditioning on a copy forces exactly d_a incident edges for motif role a, so the remaining degree contribution is Binomial(n-1-d_a,p). Dividing its mass by the unconditional Binomial(n-1,p) mass yields (k)_{d_a}/((n-1)_{d_a}p^{d_a}). Summation proves the exact formula. For regular motifs the falling factorial is strictly increasing on the relevant real interval, and direct expansion gives the asymptotic root location.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Neither marginal result determines the cross-covariance. The identity requires conditioning the degree of a host vertex on the presence of a specific motif copy and summing over motif roles. Triangle-indicator covariance matrices likewise do not imply the degree-count formula.

originality.rationale: The two closest fully inspected primary sources treat degree counts and triangle counts separately. Candidate-specific semantic and web searches did not locate the exact degree-class/motif covariance or its regular-motif sign universality. A broad 1990 random-graph functional-limit paper was only abstract-accessible and is retained as a residual risk rather than being declared non-covering.
residual_risks: Janson's broad 1990 random-graph-statistic paper was not available in full text in the inspected source and may contain an orthogonal-decomposition route implying the covariance identity.
A textbook treatment of random graph statistics may present the same covariance as an exercise or an immediate consequence of a general Hoeffding decomposition.
The originality claim is the exact finite formula together with regular-motif sign universality and threshold location, not the marginal distribution theory for degree counts or subgraph counts.

value.rationale: Degree-class frequencies and motif counts are canonical network statistics. The result gives a single finite formula for their dependence and identifies a non-obvious universality: all d-regular motifs have the same normalized covariance sign profile, with a threshold near the mean degree and an explicit constant correction. This structural relation is more informative than a one-off covariance calculation.
